predictions.hrExplainer: <0>HR-modelled</0> fits your pace against heart rate across {{n}} runs and extrapolates to threshold effort (~{{thr}} bpm) — so easy runs handled well count too, not just your fastest day.

predictions.hrLockedNoData: The HR-based estimate needs your max HR in Settings and runs logged with an average heart rate. Nothing recorded one yet.
predictions.hrLockedFew: The HR-based estimate needs {{runs}} more run(s) with an average heart rate in this period. Widen the period above if you have older ones.
predictions.hrLockedSpread: Your HR-logged runs all sit at much the same effort. About {{bpm}} bpm more range between your easiest and hardest run unlocks the HR-based estimate.
predictions.hrLockedFlat: Across these runs your pace doesn't get faster as your heart rate rises, so there is nothing to project to threshold effort yet.
predictions.hrLockedScatter: Your pace at a given heart rate is still too scattered to project from. Runs with walk breaks or long stops are the usual cause.

info.title: How predictions work
info.label: How does this work?
info.intro: Predictions project your finish time at each distance from the runs you've actually logged. Two independent methods are shown so you can sanity-check one against the other.
info.riegelP1: Both estimates extrapolate a known time to a new distance with Peter Riegel's endurance model:
info.riegelP2: The <0>1.06</0> exponent is the standard fatigue factor: going further costs slightly more than linear time, because you can't hold a 5 km pace for 20 km.
info.bestBody: Picks your single <0>strongest run</0> (≥ 3 km with a time) and projects it to every distance. It isn't simply your fastest pace — a quick 1 km blip shouldn't outrank a strong 12 km — so each run is first normalised to its Riegel-equivalent 10 km time, and the best one wins.
info.hrP1: Fits a line through <0>pace vs. heart rate</0> across your runs that recorded HR, then reads off the pace you could hold at threshold effort (~88–90% of your heart-rate reserve, roughly a one-hour race) and projects that with Riegel. Recovery-zone sessions sit out — they're walk-paced, so a couple of them would tilt the whole line — and so does any run far slower than your own median, since walk breaks and long stops drop the pace without dropping the heart rate.
info.hrP2: This rewards efficiency: a fast pace held at a low HR pulls the estimate quicker, so your easy runs count too — not just your single best day. Most logs are all easy runs inside a 15–20 bpm window, where the line your data draws is mostly noise, so its steepness is blended with a typical physiological one — the more spread and the cleaner your efforts, the more your own data decides. Reading a line off past the end of your data is still the risky part, so the estimate never reaches more than 8 bpm beyond your hardest logged effort, and it only appears once ≥ 8 HR runs, a real spread of efforts, and a tight enough result back it up.
info.elevBody: Hills make a run slower than its flat twin, so each metre climbed is credited as ~8 extra flat metres before the maths runs. This stops hilly runs from looking unfit. Listed times are for a flat course; the <0>race-day row</0> adds back your course's climb once you set it in the Plan.
info.footer: These are projections from past efforts, not promises — treat them as a fitness gauge that sharpens as you log more runs.

predictions.climbUnknown: Projected as flat — we have no climb on record for this race.
predictions.gradeNote: Runs are grade-adjusted for elevation gain. Listed times are for a flat course, except a race card with a climb on record.

info.title: How heart-rate zones work
info.label: How are they calculated?
info.intro: Your zones use the <0>Karvonen method</0>: each zone is a share of your heart-rate reserve, the gap between your resting and maximum heart rate. The same zones set your plan's session targets, the live recorder's zone readout, each run's time in zones and what the coach sees.
info.formula: Zone bpm = Rest HR + % × (Max HR − Rest HR)
info.formulaP: Working from the reserve rather than a plain percentage of max HR puts your zones higher than %-of-max apps do, and makes them your own: a lower resting heart rate widens the reserve, which spreads the zones out and moves them down slightly.
info.yours: On your profile: reserve = {{max}} − {{rest}} = {{hrr}} bpm, so the top of Zone 2 is {{rest}} + {{pct}}% × {{hrr}} = {{top}} bpm.
info.noProfile: Add your max and resting heart rate in Settings → Training profile to see your own numbers here.
info.badProfile: Your resting heart rate needs to be below your max heart rate for the zones to be calculated.
info.sessions: Easy runs, long runs and cross-training target Zone 2, tempo runs Zones 3–4, interval reps Zones 4–5, and walks Zone 1.
info.inputsMax: Max HR is the value you entered. If you left it blank or chose "I don't know my heart rate", it's estimated from your age with Tanaka's formula (208 − 0.7 × age), which can be off by 10 bpm or more either way. The highest heart rate you've seen at the end of a hard race or an all-out hill effort is a better value.
info.inputsRest: Rest HR is your heart rate on waking, before you get up; 60 bpm is assumed when it's blank.
info.otherP1: There's no single standard. Apps that use a plain percentage of max HR put the top of Zone 2 lower (often 70% of max). Apps and coaches that anchor on your lactate threshold, from a lab test or a watch's threshold test, usually put it higher, near the point where your breathing first deepens: often around 75–80% of reserve in a trained runner.
info.otherP2: Ours sit at the cautious end: they keep easy runs truly easy, which is where most of your aerobic base is built. If staying in Zone 2 feels too easy for a run where you can still talk in full sentences, your real threshold probably sits higher than the formula assumes.

planInfo.title: How your plan is built
planInfo.label: How is this built?
planInfo.intro: Your plan is generated from three inputs — your <0>race date</0>, your <1>goal time / distance</1>, and the <2>days you can train</2>. Everything below is derived from those; nothing is hand-picked.
planInfo.s1P1: Your goal time ÷ distance gives the pace you need on race day. If the course climbs, each metre of ascent is counted as ~8 extra flat metres, so a hilly goal demands the fitness of a faster flat runner. That <0>flat-equivalent target pace</0> anchors every session.
planInfo.s1P2: From the target pace we derive the training paces:
planInfo.s1Easy: <0>Easy</0> ≈ target × 1.25 — conversational, builds the aerobic engine
planInfo.s1Intervals: <0>Intervals</0> ≈ target pace — race effort in short reps
planInfo.s2P1: The calendar between next Monday and your race is split into 4–24 weeks, grouped into four phases that shift the emphasis over time:
planInfo.s2Base: <0>Base</0> (first ~4 weeks) — easy volume only, laying foundation
planInfo.s2Build: <0>Build</0> (middle block) — tempo and interval sessions alternate week to week
planInfo.s2Peak: <0>Peak</0> (final weeks before taper) — highest volume and sharpest workouts
planInfo.s2Taper: <0>Taper</0> (last 3 weeks) — volume drops to ~85 / 65 / 45% so you arrive fresh
planInfo.s3Body: Your longest available day becomes the <0>long run</0>; its distance grows week to week and is capped by the minutes you said you have (time ÷ easy pace). Your other days become the <1>quality</1> sessions — easy in base/taper, tempo or intervals in build. Every distance is clamped so a session never exceeds the time you committed to.
planInfo.footer: Changing the goal, date, elevation, or training days and regenerating rebuilds the whole schedule from scratch.
